Mission

Floating infrastructure for adapting to, and mitigating, climate change and sea level rise.

SeaBrick Society exists to make it possible for coastal communities to build on the water with materials and methods that are light on the planet, open to everyone and proven to be safe.

The problem we work on

More than a tenth of the world's population lives within ten metres of sea level. The sea is rising and will keep rising for centuries, whatever happens to emissions now, and the storms that drive water over the shore are getting stronger. Most coastal infrastructure was designed for a fixed waterline. Raising it, armouring it or moving it inland is slow, expensive and, in many places, simply not possible.

At the same time, the usual way to build in the sea, with steel and reinforced concrete, carries a large carbon cost and a short life in salt water. We think the sea deserves better materials.

Our approach

SeaBrick is a modular approach to floating infrastructure. Instead of a single large hull, structures are assembled from many small, buoyant, interlocking bricks. That has consequences we care about:

  • Communities can build it. No heavy equipment, no deep foundations, no dry dock. Bricks can be made close to where they are used and assembled by hand.
  • Structures can change. A dock can grow, a platform can be reshaped, a damaged brick can be swapped. Floating structures rise with the water as a matter of course.
  • Materials can be low-carbon. The current strategy uses mineral binders and short plant fibres rather than Portland cement, with the goal of a material far below the emissions of marine concrete.
  • Failure is local. Many small sealed units are more forgiving than one large hull: damage to a brick is damage to a brick.

What the Society does

Research

Materials, connections and marine durability, with university partners and independent engineers. We publish what we learn, including what did not work.

Standards

A definition of what a SeaBrick is: dimensions, connections, performance tests. The point is that others can build with the system and improve it.

Pilots

Small real-world structures with coastal partners: work floats, aquaculture platforms, docks. The first market for floating infrastructure is working infrastructure.

Community

Open days, model bricks, students and advisors. A building system people can hold in their hands is one they can understand and question.

Our principles

  1. Say what we know. Lab results are lab results. A material that has not been through marine exposure testing is not a marine product, and we do not describe it as one.
  2. No petrochemical shortcuts. Coatings and sealants must not shed microplastics into the sea. That bar has cost us time; we keep it.
  3. Carbon honesty. We aim for a material with far lower emissions than concrete. Whether a finished brick is fully carbon-negative depends on feedstock, energy and coating life, and we will only claim it when it is measured.
  4. The standard belongs to everyone. The Society keeps the research record and the standard in public hands. Related companies may make and sell bricks; the Society does not.
